content: The Commission on Narcotic Drugs (CND) serves as the primary policymaking body for drug control within the United Nations system. Its origins trace back to the Advisory Committee on the Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs, which was established by the League of Nations on December 15, 1920. The Advisory Committee held its first meeting from May 2 to May 5, 1921, and continued its work until 1940. The CND itself was created in 1946 by the United Nations Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), with Charles Henry Ludovic Sharman of Canada serving as its inaugural chairperson. The Commission plays a critical role in implementing international drug control treaties, including the authority to amend the schedules of controlled substances. The powers of the CND are defined by international drug control treaties, which allocate responsibilities between the Commission and the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB). The CND has the authority to influence drug control policy by advising other bodies and determining the classification of substances under control. However, enforcement powers are reserved for the INCB. Under Article 8 of the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, the CND is empowered to amend the schedules of controlled substances, draw the INCB’s attention to relevant matters, recommend measures for implementing the Convention’s objectives (including scientific research and information exchange), and notify non-parties of its decisions and recommendations to encourage their compliance. Under Article 17 of the Convention on Psychotropic Substances, the CND can amend the schedules of psychotropic substances by a two-thirds majority vote. It may also consider all matters related to the Convention’s aims and implementation and make recommendations accordingly. While the United Nations General Assembly has the authority to modify the CND’s decisions, this does not extend to scheduling decisions. The CND plays a pivotal role in drug scheduling. The Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs (Article 3) and the Convention on Psychotropic Substances (Article 2) outline the procedures for scheduling drugs, granting the CND the authority to decide the appropriate schedule for a substance. However, ECOSOC retains the power to alter or reverse the CND’s scheduling decisions. Additionally, the World Health Organization (WHO) must provide specific scientific findings regarding a substance before it can be placed in a schedule. The relationship between the WHO and the CND is defined in the Commentary on the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs. Furthermore, Article 12 of the United Nations Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances grants the CND the authority to determine whether a precursor substance used in illicit drug manufacturing should be controlled and, if so, under which category (Schedule I or II). The INCB’s scientific findings on such substances are binding on the CND, but ECOSOC retains the ability to review and overturn the CND’s decisions regarding precursor control. The CND is composed of 53 member states, each serving a four-year term. Membership is distributed geographically as follows: 11 seats for African states, 11 for Asian states, 10 for Latin American and Caribbean states, 7 for Eastern European states, 14 for Western European and other states, and 1 rotating seat alternating between Asian and Latin American/Caribbean states every four years. Members are elected from among United Nations member states, specialized agency members, and parties to the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, 1961. Elections consider the representation of countries significant in opium or coca leaf production, narcotic drug manufacturing, or those facing major issues with drug addiction or illicit trafficking. Geographic equity is also a guiding principle. The composition of the CND, being state-based rather than individual-based, makes it more susceptible to political influence, allowing governments to shape its decisions in alignment with their policies and laws. The CND’s annual meetings provide a platform for nations to debate international drug policy. For example, at the 2005 meeting, countries such as France, Germany, the Netherlands, Canada, Australia, and Iran opposed the United Nations’ zero-tolerance approach to drug policy. However, their appeal was vetoed by the United States, while the United Kingdom delegation remained reserved. A notable clash occurred between John P. Walters, Director of the U.S. Office of National Drug Control Policy, and Antonio Maria Costa, Executive Director of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, over needle exchange programs. Walters advocated for strict prohibition, while Costa emphasized the importance of providing opportunities for addicts to remain HIV-negative. The Bulletin on Narcotics has documented the CND’s activities since 1949.
